to the Bodhisattva...
1. Oṃ, homage to the glorious Vajrasattva.
[... these three verses missing from the Sanskrit ...

In the maṇḍala of the yogins and yoginīs, the one who observes the pledge (samayin) and the practitioner (sādhaka) must certainly perform the ritual actions, especially those that bring about the desired results.
In the maṇḍala of the yogas and yoginīs,
the practitioner and the initiate must especially perform the rite of bali offering as an absolute necessity.
On the fourteenth day of the full moon,
having worshipped the Yoginī in the house, one should thereafter begin the bali offering.
On the eighth day of both the bright and dark fortnights, on the full moon, and on the fourteenth day,
one should worship the Yoginī in one's own home and afterwards commence the bali offering;
likewise, one should worship the deity of the threshold on one's own side as well as outside.
Having worshipped at places such as a solitary tree with offerings and oblations,
one should likewise worship the deity of the threshold on one's own side and outside.
Having worshipped at places such as solitary trees with an offering of *bali*,
one should worship all the *yoginīs* with that very mantra. Indeed,
even if they do not understand the meaning of that mantra, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrin*) should wander about.
One should worship all the yoginīs with that very mantra;
those who do not know the meaning of that mantra [should perform] the recitation outside by the practitioner.
The deities are not satisfied even by propitiation for hundreds of millions of eons;
therefore, O Blessed One, this has always been concealed in all the tantras.
The deities are not satisfied even by propitiation for hundreds of millions of eons.
Therefore, the Blessed One has always kept this concealed within all the tantras.
For the sake of attaining accomplishment, beings who delight in Yoga Tantra—
listen now, O auspicious one, as I speak, having made it manifest.
For the sake of sentient beings devoted to Yoga Tantra who seek the cause for attaining accomplishment, I shall now reveal it; listen, O auspicious one, as I speak.
The formula for the worship of Oṃkāra: [It should be performed] in front of a solitary tree and so forth;
in a place situated within an enclosure, free from other trees;
the external worship of Oṃkāra is likewise in front of a solitary tree and so forth.
It stands within the interior of the treasury, secluded from other trees.
On a single tree, [the state] of all is spoken of, yet it is not understood.
The body is said to be the tree, joined with the branches of the hands and so forth.
"On a single tree" is spoken of for all, yet it is not understood.
The body is said to be a tree, with the hands and fingers joined as its branches.
In the Vedāntas and in the various Tantras and Āgamas,
they speak of the imperishable Aśvattha tree, whose roots are above and whose branches are below.
And in the Vedāntas and in various other Tantras, the Imperishable One declares: "The root is above, the branches are below; it is unstable."
Adorned with fruits and flowers, it is called by the name "tree";
one would not know this hidden tree established within the center of the body.
Adorned with fruits and flowers, it is called by the name "tree."
One should know the secret tree situated within the center of the body.
Four finger-breadths below the navel, there the trunk is established;
from that, three upward-reaching branches arise, joined with the *bindu* and the *koṭara*.
Four finger-breadths below the navel, the *tantrakaṇḍu* is established;
from it, three upward-reaching branches arise, joined with the *bindu* and the hollow (*koṭara*).

The three semi-vowels (*antasthā*) are said to reside in the navel, the heart, and the eyebrows; the *bindu* is likewise described [as being there]. It is said to move upward, move downward, and to have ten branches.
The three semi-vowels are said to reside in the navel, the secret place, and the eyebrows; the *bindu* is likewise described [as being there].
It is said to be upward-moving, downward-moving, and also the ten-fold one.
The flower and fruit are always present at all times, beautifully adorned with eight petals;
when the vital breath has gone to destruction, it is said that "the tree is broken.
The flower and fruit are always present at all times, beautifully adorned with eight petals.
When the breath has not yet arrived, it is said that the tree is broken.
The secret tree, the great tree, is situated at the place of the cowherds;
that tree is not known at all by the heretics, the Śrāvakas, and the like.
The secret tree, the great tree, is established at the place of the cowherds.
That tree is not known at all by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) or the disciples (*śrāvaka*) and others;
it stands situated in the midst of the great garden of Dharmodayā,
adorned with the production of fruit through the [practice of] the *śūla* and the *sūkṣma*.
In the great garden of Dharmodayā, it is firmly established in its center.
Adorned with fruits and blossoms such as white and red flowers, by resorting to that, the accomplishment of liberation arises for yogins. || 1 ||
By relying upon that, the accomplishment of liberation arises for yogins.
By the grace of the Guru’s feet, I now reveal [this];
by the grace of the Guru, I now reveal it.
The syllable *śa* is said to be semen (*śukra*), and the syllable *ma* is designated as blood (*rakta*).
The combination of these two syllables is conceived as the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
The letter *śa* is said to be semen (*śukra*), while *ma* should be known as the cremation ground, the forest of ancestors (*pitṛvana*), which is called the abode of the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
By which [knowledge] the Father reveals the play of form and beauty;
the three forms are like mothers, and the three are like fathers.
This body, composed of six sheaths, is proclaimed to be a cremation ground.
Therefore, the body of embodied beings is called "pitṛvana" (the cemetery of the fathers),
for upon the dissolution of the ten [faculties] beginning with the senses, it goes to its state of absorption.
Because its nature is characterized by destruction and the like, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is said to be the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
That which is joined with the *āśloka* is indeed that very one of secret form;
for within the element of the lotus of wisdom (*prajñāpadma*), the *pretī* is characterized by grasping.
The charnel ground (*śmaśāna*) is conceived as the place where all beings pass away. o ||
"Mountain" (parvata) is said to be the mountain that is the abode of the gods;
"mountain" is also said to be the body, which is composed of three joints (parvan),
teeming with the birds of the senses and crowded with the wild beasts of the sense-objects.
One should worship the deities of the body-mountain with offerings and oblations;
having resorted to this, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is sustained.
It is endowed with fruit-bearing trees and covered with rows of grass and hair.

Joined with flowing water, it is practiced by the Yoginīs for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*). The letter *pa* is said to be the lotus (*padma*), while the letter *va* is the face (*vaktra*). The letter *ta*, however, is great bliss (*mahāsaukhya*); therefore, it is the mountain (*parvata*).
Where there is indeed a portion of the mountain with a waterfall carrying water,
there one should worship the wise one who dwells among the gods.
By means of the nine locations beginning with the *sroha*, there is a manifold variety of supports;
therefore, it is called a "cave" (*kandara*), yet the body itself is not the cave. The letter *ka* is the body, and the letter *ā* is maintained by the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*).
Therefore, it is called *kandara*, the hollow of the vital breath (*prāṇa-kandara-kandara*).

They call the *kandara* the *bhaga* (the womb), because it is the vessel from which the nectar of flowing gnosis (*sravat-jñānāmṛta*) issues. All the limbs melt away, established in the form of semen.
The letter *ka* is in the form of intoxication (*mada*), the letter *da* is of the nature of piercing (*dāraṇa*), and the letter *ra* is by way of being the essence (*rasibhāva*);
thus it is called "Kandara."
And that which is called "Secret" (guhya) will be explained by means of which the abode of practice is desired; where the residence of eighty million yogins is conceived as being [located],
there, by the name "Secret," the very body itself is proclaimed.
From the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, she remains at the end in the form of pervasion;
abiding eternally in the form of wind, she is called the "Dweller in the Cave. The gods, both manifest and unmanifest, abide as hidden within all that is moving and unmoving.
In all the tantras, that which is concealed is called the secret. o ||
One should worship [the goddesses] with the *balicāli* offering at Janasthāna, on the outskirts of the village;
they are situated on the side of the body amidst the crowd of the senses and should be worshipped with effort through the contemplation of them as one's own presiding deities (*svādhidevatā*).

That channel which is situated at the side or the edge of a village, a body, or a human habitation is called the "village-side" (grāmapārśva). It is that place where one goes, which arises from the presiding presence of people.
Furthermore, whatever is spoken by the name of the village, or that which arises from ignorance—
whether at a single tree, a double-crested place, a triple-crested place, or at a crossroads—
one should worship the deities residing on the road with offerings preceded by bali-oblations.

The path, which resides within the body and is connected to the ten functions, should always be known by yogis as being threefold: first, as the single state of absolute oneness (*kaivalya*); second, as that which arises from the division into two; and third, as that which exists through further differentiation.
The "threefold path" (tripatha) is said to consist of the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*.
The "fourfold path" (catuṣpatha) should be known as consisting of the fourfold [mantras] beginning with *ambaka*.
It is proclaimed as the threefold path through the distinctions of downward, upward, and so forth.
The path of Brahmā is to be known as being above; below, the path of Viṣṇu is spoken of;
one should understand Rudra to be in the middle—these three are held to be the paths.
Endowed with the qualities of the square, it is situated within the secret lotus.
The three peaks and the three paths are to be known as having a dual nature and proceeding in two ways; yet,
when the meditative cultivation has entered into a state of oneness,
it should be known as the single path by virtue of its established nature as liberation.
Wherever one reaches the field that constitutes the eighth station, there perishes [all evil]. Likewise, at Ahicchatrācaritra, Kolāgiri, Jayantī, Ujjayinī, Prayāga, and Avaruṇa.
Koṭivarṣa and likewise eight others are proclaimed as this sacred field (kṣetra). Having reached the location of these, one should conquer with the *balicālinī*.
The secondary field (*upakṣetra*) is declared to be the vicinity (*upasamīpa*) of these fields.

At the site of Aṭṭahāsamukha, Caritra is located between the eyebrows;
at Kolākarṇa, the famous Jayantī is Paṇḍikā;
and at the site of Aṭṭahāsamukha, Caritra is above the eyebrows.
In the Kollākarṇa region, they are renowned as Jayātā, with their tips fashioned together.
Śāntā is at the tip of the nose, born of Prayāga;
Varuṇā is to be known as being in the two eyes; Koṭīvarṣa is at the head. One [tīrtha] is said to be at the root of the ear, and [another], born of Prayāga, is at the tip of the nose.
Varuṇā is to be known as the two eyes; Koṭīvarṣa is at the head.
Sandohā and Saṃśayā are said to be situated in the secret lotus (*guhyapadma*). [The petals are] the filaments and the pericarp... the petals... [and so forth].
She who is proclaimed as the collection of all doubts is established in the secret lotus.
It is endowed with a pericarp and filaments, and adorned with eight petals.
Furthermore, she should be known as eightfold, accompanied by Jñāneśvarī.
The field (*kṣetra*) is said to be the body, and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are proclaimed to be the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). o ||
Nevertheless, she should be known as eightfold, endowed with the Goddess of Knowledge.
The field has been called the body, and the knower of the field is proclaimed to be the vital breath.

A "void abode" (śūnyālaya) is described as one that is entirely devoid of all human beings; it is said that one should worship the deities residing therein according to the prescribed rites. A "void abode" is described as one that is unfit for the service of all humans.
The gods are established in them according to the former ordinances and ritual procedures.
The body is said to be empty, devoid of all phenomenal existence. Within the body, which is like an empty house or a dwelling, through the cultivation of the presence of the deity,
the body is declared to be empty, free from every form of conceptualization.
In an empty house or a dwelling, one should cultivate the state of being the deity within the body.
The yogin should always worship with the sixfold [practices] beginning with various forms of worship;
he should always worship the void, because of its invisible nature, and likewise the tenth channel, with the sixfold [practices] beginning with various forms of worship.
It is empty because its form is invisible, and it is indeed the tenth channel.
Having established gnosis here, one should worship with those arising from the mind;
in whatever place it is established by means of the emptiness-gnosis-vajra,
having established gnosis here, one should worship with those arising from the mind.
In whatever place she is established by means of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness.
In a house known as the Source of Phenomena (dharmodayā), through the arising of primordial wisdom and discerning knowledge,
one should worship the Goddess residing there with flowers and water.
In the abode known as Dharmodayā, which is the source of both primordial wisdom and discursive consciousness.
Then the Goddess, established in her place, should be worshipped with water and flowers by the practitioners for the sake of attaining accomplishment, in whatever vessel they may be;
they call that vessel "the secret, the external, and the intermediate."
Practitioners worship it wherever they may be for the sake of attaining accomplishment.
Regarding that, they say it is the vessel; the secret and the external are the middling ones.
Having resorted to these nine states, one attains the supreme goal.
For one situated in the ocean of saṃsāra, that [attainment] is the reaching of dry land, a stone of firm ground.
Having relied upon these ninety topics, one attains the supreme goal.
Having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra, he stands on the shore, having reached dry land;
today he is endowed with the eightfold joy and possessed of the perfection of good intelligence.
The field is said to be eightfold, yet it is traditionally remembered as having nine fields.
[These consist of] the eight stages beginning with *muditā* (joy), together with the ninth, *sādhumatī* (the stage of excellent intelligence).
Thus, the field is said to be eightfold, while the first of the nine fields is traditionally known [as the foundation].
That which is known as the mantra-vital breath, called the seed-syllable, is to be understood as the Supreme Lord. O ||
The pride of intoxication is non-conceptualization; he alone is the Holder of the Vajra.
The life-force of intoxication, which is unknowable and called "the living soul," is the Supreme Lord.
Intoxication, the state of being intoxicated, and egoism—these indeed are the great Vajradhara.
Madana is situated at the crown; she pervades from the soles of the feet to the crown.
Madāvahā is at the waist; through her, the three worlds are deluded.
Madana is situated at the crown; she pervades from the soles of the feet to the crown.
In the place of *ṭaṭi*, there is *madāvahā* (the bringer of intoxication), which deludes the three worlds;
likewise, the six elements beginning with earth are established in the form of intoxication.
Likewise, the earth and the other elements are established in the form of the six flavors;
it is said that the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) grant the eight supernatural powers (aiśvarya) and the eight accomplishments (siddhi).
by means of the accomplishment of the soft [and other stages], through wisdom, for those who accomplish [it];
because his body is intoxicated with pride, he is therefore called a *mātaṅga* (elephant).
The practitioner of mantra should constantly worship [the deity] with his own [mantras], consisting of five times five.
Having attained these positions, it is proclaimed among the deities.
beginning from the direction of Indra and so forth, as far as the domain of Īśāna.
Therefore, it should be understood through the detailed sequence of the right and left [channels].
First, Kṛṣṇarudra is situated on the big toe;
he is proclaimed by the goddesses as Kālāgnirudra.
O Mahārudra, you who abide in anger, all-pervading one whose form is the downward breath.
The god, situated in the navel, [manifests] by means of the arrangement of his illusory forms.
Having established in his heart the one named Kṛṣṇa, who is both supreme and non-supreme Mahāmāyā,
Vajrāyudha stood with great weapons at the region of Karālavadana’s face.
always standing there, terrifying and fierce, with a radiance equal to a blazing fire.
In the place of the head beyond Nanda, it has emerged from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
The goddess Nāsāturā is eternally situated with the Leader Vināyaka;
these should be installed in the intermediate directions, starting from the northeast (īśāna), in due order.
Cāmuṇḍī is situated at the location of the head, clinging to a banyan tree.
Aghoḥ is born from the triad; she is the principle of *tṛ* in the abode of the three paths.
Ghora, Mahānāma, and the others are situated at the twelve ends.
The loud-laughing one, the great destroyer, the terrible one, the fierce one, the annihilator.
the goddess Bhībhatsī, the giver of fear, is established by way of placement in the location of the heart.
She is renowned as Queen Māyā, the enchantress who deludes the world.
Umādevī, who is of a playful nature, resides in the place of intoxication as a passionate woman.
The great goddesses, Jayā and the others, abide in the form of the channels (nāḍīs).
Kālī and the others, four in number, possess great supernatural powers and are both born and yet to be born.
The deities beginning with Indra are established within the heart-lotus of the six [faces].
the six types beginning with form are established in the form of one another.
Arṇṇikā, in the form of a bee, established as Vajrasattva...
Kambojā and the others are considered the four Mahādevīs of Umānāda;
Kambojī resides in the secret place, and Dīlī is situated on the head.
burning and digesting, Maheśvarī is indeed of the nature of radiant energy.
Cūṣiṇī, Tāviryāśā, Vāyurūḍhā, and Īśvareśvarī...
[and so forth].
The goddess who is of terrible form is the Ḍākinī Licchavi;
she is of all castes,
as is Kolāgiri.
Jayantī, Alīka, and likewise Ekasvaka and Patākaka.
The markers of the eight fields.
To the east is Aṭṭahāsa; [his consort] is Saumyākṣī, with the color of molten gold; he holds a vajra in his hand and has a *kadamba* tree as his support.
In the southeast is Caritra, who is black in color, holds a spear in his hand, and has the Karañja tree as his sacred tree.
In the south is Kolāgiri, marked by a mountain; [there resides] Mahālakṣmī. [The deity there is] black in color, with a staff in hand.
In the southwest is Jayantī, with a nimba tree and a sword in hand; Jālāmukhī is smoke-colored.
In the western direction: Ujjayinī, Mahāmāyā, the Aśvattha tree, and the one with a noose in hand.
In the northwest is Vāyuvegā at Prayāga; she holds a banner in her hand, has that same color, and her tree is the Udumbara.
In the north is Śaṅkarī, holding a mace in her hand, yellow in color, and seated upon a palm tree.
In the northeast is Koṭīvarṣa; Karṇamoṭī is red in color, holds a trident in her hand, and resides in a banyan tree. o ||
The *karkaraṇḍā* is upward destruction; the *makara-rohitā* is downward destruction;
the *viccha* is sleep; *kṣum* is smoke; and *agni* is fire.
Siṃha, Mikiraḥ, Huṃ, Padma, and Pṛthivī;
Kanyā, Bhidriḥ, Śvetā, Suṃ, and Āpaḥ;
Dhanu, Kāma, Śaṅkha, Yuṃ, Vāyu, and Dakṣiṇanāśa.
Vṛṣabha-kūrma, kṣmryuṃ, rocanā, Agni; [following Mīna-bhadra etc. Kumbha-mohitā, smryuṃ, Āpaḥ, Bhūcchatrā;
Mīna-bhadra, ymryuṃ, Tṛmalā, Pṛthivī.
Gemini and Capricorn, Smṛtyuṃ, Bhaṅga, Vāyu, and Uttaranāśa.

Aḥ is consciousness (vijñāna) and wisdom (prajñā). [... This is the lineage of the Guru’s mouth; because it must be kept secret by those desiring spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*), [it should be guarded]. O ||
First, wealth should be given; second, the accumulation of wealth; third, the acquisition of fields; fourth, the sowing of seeds;
fifth, being established as a householder; sixth, the peace of the household.
Or if, on the seventh day, the meaning of what has been said does not return [to its source]. || [22x Śrī] || [End of 5]
